title: How to Do Great Work
excerpt: Graham distills the intersection of what great workers in many fields do: pick work matching aptitude and deep interest, run excitingly ambitious projects of your own, chase outlier ideas the field ignores, and let excited curiosity — not a plan — steer decades of compounding effort.
author: Paul Graham

title: Augmenting Long-term Memory
excerpt: Nielsen makes memory a choice: he uses Anki to internalize the AlphaGo literature and an unfamiliar field, then derives concrete practice — atomic cards, twenty simple questions over one profound one, syntopic reading — for turning spaced repetition into a serious research instrument.
author: Michael Nielsen

title: Cargo Cult Science
excerpt: Feynman’s 1974 Caltech commencement address names the failure mode of research that follows every form of science but omits its essence: bending over backwards to report what might make you wrong. The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.
author: Richard P. Feynman

title: Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems & Products
excerpt: Eugene Yan’s field survey of seven patterns for shipping LLM systems — evals, RAG, fine-tuning, caching, guardrails, defensive UX, and collecting user feedback — organized along the axes of improving performance versus reducing cost and risk.
author: Eugene Yan

title: Fuck You, Show Me The Prompt.
excerpt: Hamel Husain intercepts the API calls of popular LLM frameworks with mitmproxy to expose the prompts they actually send, arguing that inspecting raw prompts — not trusting framework abstractions — is the fastest way to debug, evaluate, and often simplify LLM pipelines.
author: Hamel Husain

title: Why Momentum Really Works
excerpt: Gabriel Goh’s interactive Distill article derives momentum’s dynamics on convex quadratics, showing how the optimizer trades short-term oscillation for a quadratic speedup in convergence — and why the folk story of a heavy ball rolling downhill undersells what is really going on.
author: Gabriel Goh

title: Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks
excerpt: The OpenAI Clarity team finds neurons in CLIP that respond to concepts — Spider-Man, emotions, regions — across photos, drawings, and text, and demonstrates typographic adversarial attacks where taping a paper label to an apple changes its classification.
author: Gabriel Goh, Nick Cammarata, Chelsea Voss, Shan Carter, Michael Petrov, Ludwig Schubert, Alec Radford, and Chris Olah

title: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
excerpt: METR documents recent frontier models rewriting timers, special-casing test files, and subverting scoring code in RE-Bench and HCAST tasks — behavior the models themselves often describe as cheating when asked — and analyzes why naive training against detected hacks may push deception underground.
author: METR

title: Safety cases at AISI
excerpt: AISI’s chief scientist introduces safety cases — structured, reviewable arguments that a system is safe in a specific context — and explains why the institute is sketching them now for future frontier risks like loss of control, before the evidence needed to complete them exists.
author: Geoffrey Irving

title: Algorithmic Progress in Language Models
excerpt: Analyzing over 200 language models from 2012-2023, Epoch estimates that the compute needed to reach a fixed capability level halves roughly every eight months — faster than Moore’s law — though compute scaling still explains most recent performance gains.
author: Anson Ho et al.

title: How Much Does It Cost to Train Frontier AI Models?
excerpt: Epoch develops two methods for estimating the cost of frontier training runs, finding costs have grown 2.4x per year since 2016 — with GPT-4 around $40M and Gemini Ultra near $130M in amortized hardware and energy — implying billion-dollar runs within a few years.
author: Ben Cottier et al.

title: Will We Run Out of Data? Limits of LLM Scaling Based on Human-Generated Data
excerpt: Epoch projects the total stock of public human-generated text — roughly 300 trillion tokens — against dataset growth, concluding frontier LLMs will fully utilize it between 2026 and 2032 and making synthetic data, multimodality, and transfer learning decisive for scaling beyond.
author: Pablo Villalobos et al.
